overview: This atlas record concerns the eighteenth-century Kingdom of Ireland, not medieval Gaelic kingdoms or today's Irish state. Its parliament and social institutions existed within a monarchy shared with Britain. The map continues the label to 1815, although the separate Irish parliament ended when the union took effect in 1801.

periods.title: A kingdom with unequal political power
periods.summary: Irish parliamentary life operated within restrictions that became targets of reform campaigns.

periods.title: Legislative change and crisis
periods.summary: Parliament obtained greater legislative autonomy in 1782; the rebellion of 1798 was followed by renewed pressure for union.

periods.title: After parliamentary union
periods.summary: Ireland became part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; the later map segment is not a separate kingdom's continuing parliament.

items.text: The Irish Volunteers, formed in 1778, pressed for changes to restrictions on Irish commerce. In 1782 British ministers accepted major legislative changes. These developments concerned political and commercial power, not equal voting rights for every resident.
The 1800 union legislation was debated and approved before it came into force on 1 January 1801. Keeping the law's passage and implementation separate helps explain why sources give both years.

Marsh's Library opened under an Act of 1707 to give readers a place to study. Its first librarian, Élie Bouhéreau, was a Huguenot refugee from France. A Dublin institution preserved books and expertise carried across borders.

By the mid 1760s, more than 1000 books had disappeared from Marsh's. Readers were then supervised at a table or locked into reading cages. The librarian's solution to book theft was considerably more dramatic than a reminder email.

Bartholomew Mosse founded Dublin's lying-in hospital in 1745 to provide maternity care and training. It moved to the present Rotunda site in 1757. These buildings document an organized response to childbirth needs, not proof that every mother could obtain safe care.
Plays, performances of Handel's music and lotteries raised money for the new maternity hospital. Entertainment and philanthropy were connected: an evening out could help pay for wards and equipment.

Lisburn's weavers brought cloth to the market house before a separate brown-linen market was built around 1750. Making cloth and finding buyers were linked stages of work. A successful textile industry still depended on many individual households and workers.

The Royal Dublin Society, founded in 1731, offered premiums for tree planting from 1742. Awards were one way to encourage agricultural and economic experiments. They show what an institution promoted, not that every landowner followed its advice.

The Society established its drawing school in 1750, teaching figure, landscape and ornamental work; architectural drawing followed in the 1760s. Art education could support useful design and building skills as well as pictures for display.

In the early 1800s, Lisburn's market-house assembly room hosted dinners, dances, concerts and speakers. This example belongs after the 1801 union, within the atlas's later years. Changes in parliamentary government did not stop local social life.

sections.title: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller

items.text: Jonathan Swift published the book usually called Gulliver's Travels in 1726. Its invented voyages let him criticize human behaviour and institutions. It is an achievement of imaginative writing, not evidence that tiny islanders or giant people actually existed.

Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World is part of the book's original English title. Here remote means far away. This short written sample comes from a specific 1726 work; it does not imply that English was everyone's home language in Ireland.

ending.text: The separate Irish parliament ended under the union that took effect on 1 January 1801. Irish communities and institutions continued within the United Kingdom. The map's 1815 endpoint is a later coverage boundary, not the date Ireland lost its people or the year the parliamentary union began.
